title: FEAT: A Preference Feedback Dataset through a Cost-Effective Auto-Generation and Labeling Framework for English AI Tutoring
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of constructing high-quality teacher feedback data for English tutoring systems, where manual generation and ranking of feedback is expensive and time-consuming. The authors argue that scalable feedback datasets are needed to support reward-based or ranking-based learning for AI tutoring models that can provide more human-friendly guidance.

To address this, the paper proposes FEAT, a framework that uses large language models to generate teacher feedback and create preference datasets under different supervision regimes. The study constructs three datasets: DIRECT-Manual (human plus LLM generation with human rankings), DIRECT-Generated (LLM-generated and LLM-annotated preferences), and DIRECT-Augmented (a hybrid combining mostly generated data with a small amount of manual data). The framework also applies five feedback criteria—Correct, Revealing, Guidance, Diagnostic, and Encouragement—intended to make the feedback educationally appropriate.

The empirical context is English tutoring, with tutoring scenarios derived from the MCTest reading comprehension dataset, which is described as serving students in grades 1–4. The paper evaluates several ranking approaches, including binary classification, reward modeling, DPO, RankNet, and an ensemble, using open-source LLMs of 1B and 3B scale. The work is not a classroom intervention; it is a dataset and model-ranking study focused on feedback generation and preference learning.

The main conclusion is that LLM-generated preference data can perform competitively with human-annotated data, and that mixing a small amount of human-annotated data into generated data (about 5–10%) can outperform training on the fully human-annotated dataset alone. The authors conclude that FEAT can reduce human annotation cost while maintaining or improving ranking performance, and they suggest extending the framework to broader educational contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language models used for generating and ranking teacher feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as feedback-generation sources in the DIRECT-Manual and DIRECT-Generated datasets (e.g., GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o) and compared against human and other model-generated feedback for English tutoring.

findings.finding_summary: In the DIRECT-Manual dataset, GPT-4 feedback was ranked highest by humans among five candidate feedback sources (GPT-4 > Human > GPT-3.5 > PrepTutor > DIRECT) for an English tutoring example. In the ranking-model evaluation, LLM-generated feedback from GPT-family models contributed to preference data where models trained on DG or DA performed competitively with human-annotated DM, but the paper does not report separate quantitative effect sizes for ChatGPT-specific outputs beyond ranking examples and dataset construction.
findings.measure: Human-annotated feedback ranking; pairwise preference ranking model performance

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic large language models used for generating and annotating educational feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to automatically generate teacher feedback for the DIRECT-Generated dataset and as one of the LLMs contributing to the feedback pool compared in examples and dataset construction.

findings.finding_summary: Claude-generated feedback was included among LLM-generated teacher feedback candidates and was used in constructing the DIRECT-Generated dataset. The paper reports that adding a small amount of human-annotated DM data to LLM-generated DG improved ranking performance overall, but it does not isolate Claude-specific effects.
findings.measure: Preference data construction; ranking-model performance on DG/DA datasets

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta LLaMA-family large language models used for generating teacher feedback and training ranking models.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the feedback generation models for DIRECT-Generated (Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct) and as the ranking-model backbone family (Llama-1B, Llama-3B, and instruct variants) for evaluating preference datasets.

findings.finding_summary: In the DG�DM comparison, LLaMA-based ranking models trained on automatically generated DG achieved competitive performance relative to human-annotated DM baselines. The paper reports that for Llama-3B-IT, binary classifier, DPO, and ensemble approaches reached or exceeded the DM�DM baseline with only 5% human-annotated DM added to DG, and several approaches surpassed the baseline in the 5�10% range.
findings.measure: Rank-biased overlap (RBO) for pairwise ranking agreement

findings.finding_summary: When varying the proportion of human-annotated DM in DA, performance generally improved as more DM was added, and Llama-3B surpassed the DM�DM baseline in all methods with at most 10�25% DM data. This supports the paper�s conclusion that high performance can be achieved with minimal human annotation cost.

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba Qwen-family large language models used for ranking teacher feedback and preference learning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a ranking-model backbone (Qwen-3B-IT) to evaluate the quality of preference datasets and the effect of human-annotation ratios in DA.

findings.finding_summary: Qwen-3B-IT showed competitive ranking performance in the DM�DM and DG�DM settings, with DG�DM sometimes approaching DM�DM performance across ranking methods. The paper reports that Qwen-3B-IT surpassed DM�DM primarily when the DA mix contained about 50�75% or 75�100% human-annotated DM, indicating stronger gains with more human data than LLaMA-based counterparts.
findings.measure: Rank-biased overlap (RBO) for pairwise ranking agreement

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / LLM-based systems used to generate, annotate, and rank teacher feedback for tutoring.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper broadly studies an LLM-based framework (FEAT) for automatically generating teacher feedback preference datasets for English AI tutoring and comparing LLM-generated versus human-annotated feedback quality.

findings.finding_summary: Across ranking-model experiments, feedback generated by LLMs produced rankings that were highly comparable to human annotator rankings. The authors report that models trained on DG performed competitively with DM-based models, and adding only 5�10% human-annotated DM to DG yielded superior performance to using the full DM dataset alone.
findings.measure: Rank-biased overlap (RBO) of pairwise feedback rankings

findings.finding_summary: Increasing feedback criteria from two (Correct, Revealing) to five consistently improved ranking-model performance in several settings. The paper interprets this as evidence that richer feedback information improves generalization in AI-generated tutoring feedback datasets.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical NLP/education systems paper, but it is not a student learning intervention study and does not provide randomized evidence on learner outcomes. The strongest evidence concerns ranking-model performance and dataset construction quality rather than causal educational impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are about data efficiency and ranking agreement, not direct educational achievement or instructional practice outcomes. Any impact is promising but indirect and not quantified with standard educational effect sizes.
